content: 1. A preferred antiretroviral regimen for HIV treatment includes Efavirenz 600 mg orally once daily combined with Abacavir 600 mg and Lamivudine 300 mg orally once daily. This regimen is suitable only for patients who are HLA-B5701 negative and have pre-treatment HIV RNA levels below 100,000 copies/mL. 2. When Tenofovir or Abacavir cannot be used, an alternative preferred regimen includes Darunavir 800 mg and Ritonavir 100 mg orally once daily combined with Raltegravir 400 mg orally once daily. This is recommended for patients with pre-treatment HIV RNA levels below 200 cells/mm³. 3. For pediatric patients, Nevirapine dosing is weight-based: For children weighing 5 to <40 kg: 400 mg orally once daily. For children weighing ≥40 kg: 600 mg orally once daily. Maximum dose per administration is 200 mg. For children aged 1 day to 8 years: 200 mg/m²/dose orally once daily for 14 days, then 200 mg/m²/dose orally twice daily. For children aged 8 years and older: 120–150 mg/m²/dose orally once daily for 14 days, then 120–150 mg/m²/dose orally twice daily. 4. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for treatment-naive patients is lifelong. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate should be avoided in patients with creatinine clearance <50 mL/min. Rilpivirine is recommended for patients with CD4 counts >200 cells/mL and should not be used with proton pump inhibitors. Efavirenz is contraindicated in pregnant women. 5. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention involves Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg and Emtricitabine 200 mg orally once daily for up to 90 days. High-risk individuals, such as men who have sex with men, intravenous drug users, those with HIV-positive partners, or those with a history of inconsistent condom use, are advised to take PrEP. Follow-up visits every 3 months should include HIV testing, medication adherence counseling, risk reduction support, side effect assessment, STI symptom evaluation, and pregnancy testing. Renal function should be assessed at 3 months and every 6 months thereafter, and bacterial STI testing should be performed every 6 months. 6. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV involves Raltegravir 400 mg orally twice daily combined with Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg and Emtricitabine 200 mg orally once daily. Therapy should ideally begin within hours of exposure and continue for 28 days. For low-risk exposures (e.g., mucous membrane contact), regimens may include Zidovudine 100 mg and Lamivudine 300 mg orally once daily or other combinations. For high-risk exposures (e.g., percutaneous needle stick), expanded regimens may include Zidovudine, Lamivudine, and Lopinavir/Ritonavir. 7. During labor and delivery, if maternal HIV RNA is <1000 copies/mL with good adherence, the current ART regimen should be continued. If HIV RNA is >1000 copies/mL, adherence is poor, or HIV RNA levels are unknown, intravenous Zidovudine should be administered at 2 mg/kg over 1 hour, followed by 1 mg/kg/hour continuous infusion until umbilical cord clamping. 8. Postpartum, ART should be initiated or continued after delivery and breastfeeding cessation. 9. For HIV-exposed infants of mothers who received antepartum ART prophylaxis, Zidovudine (ZDV) 100 mg orally should be started at birth and continued for six weeks. Dosing is based on gestational age and weight, with initiation preferably within 6–12 hours of delivery. For infants of mothers who did not receive antepartum ART, dosing is weight-based and initiated as soon as possible after birth. 10. Prophylaxis for opportunistic infections in HIV-infected patients is based on CD4 counts and clinical history. For example, prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is indicated for CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³ or a history of AIDS-defining illness. Preferred regimens include Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole, with adjunctive corticosteroids for moderate-to-severe cases. 11. For latent tuberculosis infection, treatment involves an initiation phase with Isoniazid, Rifampin or Rifabutin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol for 2 months, followed by a continuation phase with Isoniazid and Rifampin or Rifabutin for 5–7 months. 12. For Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) prophylaxis, Azithromycin 1200 mg orally once weekly or Clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily is recommended for patients with CD4 counts <50 cells/µL. Treatment for disseminated MAC includes Clarithromycin or Azithromycin combined with Ethambutol for at least 12 months. 13. For severe mucocutaneous herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections, initial therapy involves Acyclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 8 hours, transitioning to oral therapy once lesions regress. For acyclovir-resistant HSV, Foscarnet or alternative therapies like Cidofovir or topical agents are used. 14. For varicella-zoster virus (VZV) prevention, vaccination is recommended for seronegative patients with CD4 counts ≥200 cells/µL. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes Varicella-Zoster Immune Globulin (Varizig™) or antiviral therapy with Acyclovir or Valacyclovir. 15. For cryptococcal meningitis, induction therapy involves liposomal Amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy with Itraconazole 200 mg orally twice to three times daily for at least one year. 16. For histoplasmosis, induction therapy with liposomal Amphotericin B 3 mg/kg IV daily is recommended for at least 2 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy with Itraconazole 200 mg orally daily. 17. For cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, preferred regimens include intravitreal Ganciclovir injections combined with oral Valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily for 14–21 days. Alternative regimens include IV Ganciclovir, Foscarnet, or Cidofovir. 18. Annual inactivated influenza vaccination is recommended for all HIV-infected patients. Live-attenuated influenza vaccines are contraindicated. 19. For syphilis exposure, treatment involves Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly as a single dose. Alternative regimens include Doxycycline, Ceftriaxone, or Azithromycin, though Azithromycin is not recommended for men who have sex with men (MSM) or pregnant women.
